justification: The article’s spine is the step-down and the impossibility of proving it: “The maneuver is the cheap part … It was always going to be the cheap part,” followed by a whole closing section on how “a success looks like an empty picture. So does a forecast that was wrong, and a contrail too thin to register, and a sheet of cloud sitting over the top of one.” That is B. A (humidity forecasting) and C (crystal growth) are supporting paragraphs subordinate to that argument, and D’s comparison of contrail warming against fuel warming is never made anywhere in the text.

Both attributes are stated: “the layer runs a couple of hundred miles with a depth that would fit inside a small hill,” confirmed by Vestrigg’s “The layers are usually shallow enough that one step down is out of them,” and “Air can sit well past ice saturation and make no cloud of its own … So the sky stays clear.” That is A. B is contradicted by that same no-cloud sentence; C is contradicted by “a layer like that has nothing in it to look at” and “the first anyone knows of it is the mark an airplane leaves crossing it”; D attributes to the layer what the text says of the contrail, which needs time “to spread wide enough for a satellite to register it.”

The reason given for the night-only rule is the missing daytime counterweight: “a spreading contrail holds in heat that would otherwise leave, and in daylight it also turns some sunlight back toward space, so the two effects pull against one another, while after dark there is nothing pulling the other way.” That is D. C overstates the same sentence — daylight only means the two effects oppose each other, not that a contrail cools on balance. A (light night traffic) and B (deeper layers at night) are never asserted; the text says only that the layers are shallow.

The untouched flights are the calibration: “Of 141 flights that were left alone and flew straight through a forecast layer, 61 left a mark anybody could find afterward. The forecast was calling for wet air a good deal more often than the sky supplied it.” If well under half of forecast layers actually produce a contrail, then many of the 96 descents that were flown avoided nothing — C. A misreads the construction: all 141 flew through a forecast layer by definition; B inverts the direction of the error (over-calling, not missing); D is contradicted by the 61 that did leave a mark.

The writer ranks the two sources explicitly: “the satellite count is the smallest thing those two winters produced … the findings that will outlast the trial are his … The second of those comes off records the center already keeps and needed no picture at all.” That is A. C is contradicted by that ranking; D overstates it, since “A picture that shows a contrail settles that one flight” and no call is made to stop the imagery; B misassigns Vestrigg’s wish to the writer, who answers it with the noncommittal “Perhaps it would.”
